text:
COURT FILE No.:

DATE:  2010·July·7

Citation:
R. v. Lee
, 2010 ONCJ 291

ONTARIO
COURT  OF  JUSTICE

BETWEEN:

HER  MAJESTY  THE  QUEEN

—  AND  —

HAROLD LEE

Before Justice Kelly P. Wright

Heard on May 19
and June 18, 2010

Reasons for Judgment
released on July 7, 2010

P. Garcia .....................................................................................................................   for
the Crown

D. O’Connor...........................................................................................
for the accused, Harold Lee

Wright, J.:

[
1
]

Harold Lee comes before this court charged
with one count of threaten death as a result of a posting he put on his
Facebook page on November 10, 2009.

[
2
]

The evidence in this matter was heard over
the course of two days.  The Crown called three witnesses, Amanda Davey, Ken
Tooby and Sgt. Daniel Sova.    The bulk   of the Crown’s case, however, comes
before the court in the form of Harold Lee’s Facebook postings with entries
dating back to June 2007.

[
3
]

Mr. Lee testified on his own behalf.

[
4
]

This is my judgment.

[
5
]

Although the trial spanned over several
days, the facts in this case are not complicated and are not in dispute.

[
6
]

In September of 2009, York University
Security and Toronto Police Service were alerted to some disturbing and
disconcerting postings on Harold Lee’s Facebook page.  The postings included
images of swastikas, a single reference to the Virginia Tech massacre and
anti-Semitic comments.  On September 30, 2009, Mr. Lee was cautioned by Det.
Sova of the Toronto Police Service about these types of postings.  Mr. Lee
indicated that he understood and it would be wrong to continue.  No criminal
charges were laid.

[
7
]

On  November 10, 2009, Harold Lee posted the
following comment on his face book profile page:

“I’m wearing black and I’m riding black this time
around…I’m really sorry however you never thought this day would come, and
didn’t want it to be this way… I never knew why you would frame me nor put me
on the cross for a few dollars… but I don’t care, if you are a priest, judge,
cop, lawyer, commoner, or teacher… I ‘m bringing death with me this time
around.”

[
8
]

In order to find Mr. Lee guilty, I must be
convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that when he wrote these words he did so
with an intent to intimidate and/or cause fear.  The test to be applied in this
assessment is an objective one in which I must take into account the words that
were used, the context they were used in, the person(s) to whom they were directed
and the explanation offered by Mr. Lee.

[
9
]

This case is unique because the alleged
threat comes in the form of a posting that was made by Mr. Lee on his Facebook
page.  It is noteworthy that this was a posting on Mr. Lee’s Facebook page as opposed
to a message  he posted on someone else’s Facebook page.  At the time it was
made, 273 people had access to Mr. Lee’s Facebook.  These authorized
individuals are commonly known as ‘friends’ in the Facebook environment.  The
Crown alleges that all those individual or ‘friends’ that would have had access
to Mr. Lee’s Facebook were the subject of the threat.   It is noteworthy that
in order for any of his friends to read the posting they would have had to
access Mr. Lee’s Facebook page.  There is no way for Mr. Lee to confirm that a
friend has read his message unless they write a reply comment or tell him directly
that they have done so.  If Mr. Lee meant the message to be taken seriously, it
seems to me he would want to ensure that his target audience would have
received it.  The Facebook format I have reviewed, of which Mr. Lee was well
aware, diminishes the seriousness that can be attached to the words written by
Mr. Lee on this occasion.

[
10
]

I have reviewed in detail, the Facebook
entries of Mr. Lee which make up exhibits 1 and 2 on these proceedings.

[
11
]

It is clear from my review that Mr. Lee had
a habit of reporting almost hourly what he was doing, this included everything
from playing poker, studying, going to the gym or listening to music.  His
posting are littered with biblical references and his political opinions. Many
of the postings are simply random personal thoughts and others are part of a
conversation.  Mr. Lee was not shy about posting his frustration and anger
towards York University and the treatment he received while he was a student
there.   He openly admits his disdain for the police and the Jewish community.
He clearly treated Facebook as forum where he was free to write whatever came
into his mind and did so.

[
12
]

It is against this backdrop that I must
assess the words conveyed by Mr. Lee on November 10, 2009.

[
13
]

The Crown directs me to a posting in which
Mr. Lee referenced sitting outside a Toronto Courthouse.  It is difficult to
say with any accuracy when Mr. Lee made this entry in relation to the alleged
threat.  The dates and times reflected on all of the Facebook pages that
comprise exhibits 1 and 2 are confusing and difficult to follow.  However, Mr.
Lee recalls writing that message and confirms that he was outside a Toronto
courthouse on November 10, 2009 at 8:20 am when he made this entry.  He said he
was waiting to contest a parking ticket and he was listeneing to music.  I
accept his evidence in this regard.  It is consistent with his habitual
reporting of where he is and what he is doing.  Most of the words written by
him are lyrics to a song.  I find no connection between this entry and the one
in question, nor am I concerned by it.

[
14
]

The Crown further directs me to a biblical
reference about burning charity and favour, repentance and redemption.  That
entry appears to have been made within the hours following the alleged threat.
Again, Mr. Lee acknowledges the entry and explains the biblical meaning behind
it.  He goes onto say, however, that when he is smoking marijuana he feels he
himself is burning charity and favour and writes about it.  This is consistent
with other entries where Mr. Lee has referenced burning charity and favour.  I
find no connection between it and the alleged threat.

[
15
]

I will now turn to the content of the
posting that forms the basis of the charge before this court.

[
16
]

Mr. Lee testified that the posting was not a
threat at all.  He said he was simply referencing a personal experience.  He
said that he had been working for the Coroner during the H1N1 outbreak and his
job was to transport dead bodies.  He said this had a profound effect on him
and he chose to write about it.

[
17
]

This is not the first reference he makes to
this type of work.  Mr. Lee writes about working for the Coroner, the H1N1
virus and picking up dead bodies earlier in September of 2009 on Facebook.  It
is not unreasonable that this would have had a profound effect on him.  Nor is
it unreasonable for Mr Lee to write about.  It seems to be common practice for
him to write about every experience he has had, from the mundane to the
extraordinary.  This consistency adds a degree of believability to his
explanation.

[
18
]

Twice in that message, Mr. Lee references
the colour black which is often associated with death.  In this case, Mr. Lee
said he wrote he was wearing black because the uniform he was wearing was
black.  In my review of his Facebook messages, Mr. Lee routinely reported on
the most insignificant details, so the fact that on this occasion he mentioned
the colour of his clothes is of no moment.  He also said he was riding black.  I
am not prepared to read some nefarious intent into this reference.  In July of
2009, Mr. Lee posted that he was riding black again after having had a pale
grey ride for 6 years.  I am assuming this is a reference to a vehicle which
would be consistent with the November 10, 2009 posting.

[
19
]

Mr. Lee makes a biblical reference in this
posting.  Again, this is common for Mr. Lee as he seems to view life through a
religious lens.  His Facebook is replete with religious messages many of which
reference death in some way.  It is how he thinks and communicates. The Crown
challenged him on the validity of this particular reference.  Mr. Lee was able
to direct her to the exact passage in the bible to which he was referring.
His ability to accurately recall and reference the biblical passage adds a
layer of believability to his explanation.

[
20
]

It is an undisputed fact that Mr. Lee was
working for the Coroner during the H1N1 virus outbreak and it was his job was
to transport dead bodies.    Again, this adds to the believability of his
explanation.

[
21
]

Absent this explanation, it is easy to see
how this posting could have been interpreted as a threat.

[
22
]

The question becomes whether I accept Mr.
Lee’s explanation or even if  I don’t, am left in a reasonable doubt because
of  it.

[
23
]

His evidence was not without its
difficulties.  Mr. Lee was confusing and difficult to follow at times.  He is
clearly a troubled individual.  Many of his postings on Facebook are offensive,
disturbing and deplorable.  But as upsetting and disconcerting as they may be,
they do not form the basis of any criminal charge that is before me for consideration.
Nor do I find a connection between them and the posting on November 10, 2009.
The context of threat combined with Mr. Lee’s explanation as to when and why he
wrote the message has left me in a state of reasonable doubt.

[
24
]

After a thorough review of all the evidence,
the law and the submissions of counsel I am not convinced beyond a reasonable
doubt that when  Mr. Lee posted the message on November10, 2009 on his Facebook
he intended it as a threat.

[
25
]

Accordingly, Mr. Lee, I find you not guilty
on the one count of threaten death.

Released:       July 7, 2010.

_________________________________

Signed:
“Justice Kelly P. Wright”
